summary:
Balıkesir is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework, in which hostility toward trans people operates as organised state policy rather than residual prejudice. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions (256 recorded through formal channels, 43 taken off the record) and systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

At the launch of that report, titled 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy', lawyer Kerem Dikmen presented findings that anti-LGBTI+ hostility has been institutionalised as explicit state policy. Senior officials' hate speech, and instructions issued to public institutions under a state-declared family year, created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

The Erdoğan government frames its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma against LGBT people. Under that framing, a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025.

That measure is the leaked 11th Judicial Package, described by Human Rights Watch in a news release of 29 October 2025 as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. It would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality; criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, with penalties of up to four years in prison; raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 on condition of permanent infertility; and punish health professionals who perform such care. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft.

The package had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them. Istanbul is one data point within a national pattern of street-level control, not an isolated locality.

Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor, any checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Kaos GL's 2025 findings record senior officials' hate speech alongside instructions issued to public institutions, and note that regulatory and supervisory bodies restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. Restrictions on performance, exhibition and public speech therefore shape what a visitor will see presented openly in any province, including Balıkesir, independent of any direct encounter with police.

The pattern has a long documented history. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report, based on more than 70 interviews conducted over three years, recorded beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It is background evidence of how entrenched the regime is, not a statement of the law in force today, and the legal changes made after 2018 are not described in the sources available here.

Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the death of a transgender prisoner in parliament on 12 December 2025, and a coalition of Human Rights Association branches demanded an independent investigation. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association jointly oppose the draft 11th Judicial Package. These are signs of active opposition rather than evidence of protection.

Residents face detention at a scale that the annual reporting quantifies: 313 recorded violations in 2025 and 299 detention decisions, of which 43 were taken outside formal channels. Off-record detentions are recorded separately because they leave no official trace, which matters for anyone assessing their own exposure.

The draft 11th Judicial Package would reach residents directly through three provisions: criminalisation of behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, up to four years' imprisonment for taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony, and punishment of health professionals who provide gender-affirming care. Inside, LGBT detainees are subject to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, hospital transfers refused on grounds of other prisoners' behaviour, transfers that cut visits and solidarity networks, and complaints processes that are ineffective and may provoke further violence. outOfScopeNotes:
The 11th Judicial Package remained a draft at the time of reporting. Human Rights Watch's release is dated 29 October 2025 and describes a leaked text; whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is unresolved in the sources available here.

No Balıkesir-specific source appears in this inventory. The GBT checkpoint account, the Pride monitoring, the Sincan prison death and the Bakırköy attack all concern other provinces and are used to illustrate a national regime that applies in Balıkesir as well. Enforcement frequency, local police practice and any Pride or LGBT venue activity in Balıkesir itself are not sourced.

The September 2025 health regulation is reported through secondary coverage of a Health Ministry circular and a Kayseri provincial directive. Its precise legal text, the definition of the barred "other" option, and whether it governs private as well as public facilities are unresolved.

Whether a foreign visitor's gender marker mismatch would itself trigger refusal of entry, secondary screening or a documentation requirement beyond the standard carry-ID rule is not stated in the inventory. The sources establish that identity documents are demanded at checkpoints and that presentation may be compared against them, but no reported case of a trans visitor being refused entry on that basis is documented here.

The 2008 Human Rights Watch report is explicitly historical. It predates the legal changes made after 2018, and no source in this inventory describes the current statutory position on consensual same-sex conduct or on legal gender recognition in Turkey.
